figures.title: Serum potassium
figures.caption: Potassium has a narrow normal range, and both extremes disturb the heart's rhythm. Put the client on a cardiac monitor at either end, and never give potassium IV push.

bands.label: Critical
bands.note: Risk of respiratory muscle weakness and dysrhythmias. Replace IV on a pump with monitoring.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Weakness, leg cramps, flat T waves, U waves. Raises the risk of digoxin toxicity.

bands.label: High
bands.note: Muscle weakness, peaked T waves. Hold potassium supplements and potassium-sparing drugs.

bands.label: Critical
bands.note: Wide QRS, heart block, ventricular fibrillation. Calcium gluconate protects the heart first.

figures.title: Treating hypoglycemia: the rule of 15
figures.caption: Fast sugar first, recheck, then a snack with protein so the glucose doesn't fall again. A client who cannot swallow safely gets nothing by mouth.

steps.title: Confirm the glucose
steps.detail: Below 70 mg/dL, or classic signs (shaky, sweaty, confused) and no meter at hand: treat now, don't wait.

steps.title: Give 15 g of fast carbohydrate
steps.detail: 4 oz of juice or regular soda, or 3 to 4 glucose tablets, only if the client is awake and can swallow.

steps.title: Recheck in 15 minutes
steps.detail: Still below 70 mg/dL? Give another 15 g and recheck again.

steps.title: Add protein and a complex carbohydrate
steps.detail: Once above 70 mg/dL, a snack or the next meal keeps it from dropping again.

steps.title: Can't swallow? Nothing by mouth
steps.detail: Give glucagon IM or subcut, or dextrose 50% IV, per protocol. Turn the client on their side.

figures.title: IV fluids by tonicity
figures.caption: Tonicity decides where the water goes: isotonic fluid stays in the vessels, hypotonic moves into the cells, and hypertonic pulls water out of them. D5W is isotonic in the bag but acts hypotonic once the dextrose is used.
rows: Isotonic
0.9% saline, lactated Ringer’s. Stays in the vessels, so it expands blood volume
Fluid overload (crackles, distended neck veins), most of all in heart or kidney failure
Hypotonic
0.45% saline. Leaves the vessels and moves into cells, rehydrating them
Can drop BP and swell brain cells; avoid with head injury, stroke, burns or low sodium
Hypertonic
3% saline, D5 in 0.45% saline, D10W. Pulls water from the cells into the vessels
Overload and cell dehydration; 3% saline runs slowly on a pump with frequent sodium checks
D5W
Isotonic in the bag; once the dextrose is used, it acts like free water
Adds no sodium; can lower serum sodium and worsen brain swelling

figures.title: Serum sodium
figures.caption: Sodium problems show up in the brain, so watch mental status and take seizure precautions at either extreme. Correct a chronic imbalance slowly: raising a long-standing low sodium too fast causes osmotic demyelination.

bands.label: Critical
bands.note: Seizures, coma, respiratory arrest from brain swelling. ICU care; hypertonic 3% saline given slowly.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Headache, nausea, confusion, weakness. Restrict fluids if it is dilutional; replace sodium if it was lost.

bands.label: High
bands.note: Thirst, dry sticky mucous membranes, restlessness, agitation. Replace water gradually.

bands.label: Critical
bands.note: Lethargy, seizures, coma. Lower it slowly as ordered; dropping it too fast causes cerebral edema.

figures.title: Serum calcium and magnesium
figures.caption: Both minerals calm nerves and muscles. When either falls, muscles overreact (tingling, tetany, seizures); when either rises, reflexes and breathing slow. A low magnesium keeps potassium and calcium low until it is replaced.

bands.label: Critical
bands.note: Laryngospasm, seizures, long QT. Seizure precautions; IV calcium gluconate slowly, on a monitor.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Tingling around the mouth and fingers, cramps, brisk reflexes, positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs.

bands.label: High
bands.note: Weakness, sluggish reflexes, constipation, confusion, kidney stones. IV saline, walk, stop thiazides.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Tremors, brisk reflexes, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, torsades. Seizure precautions; replace magnesium.

bands.label: High
bands.note: Flushing, low BP, weak or absent reflexes, slow breathing, heart block. Calcium gluconate reverses it.

figures.title: Reading an arterial blood gas
figures.caption: ROME: in Respiratory problems, pH and PaCO2 move in Opposite directions; in Metabolic problems, pH and bicarbonate move the same way (Equal). If the other value has shifted to offset it, compensation has begun; a normal pH means full compensation.

bands.label: Acidosis
bands.note: Too much acid: a high PaCO2 (respiratory) or a low bicarbonate (metabolic).

bands.label: Alkalosis
bands.note: Too little acid: a low PaCO2 (respiratory) or a high bicarbonate (metabolic).

bands.label: Low: alkalotic
bands.note: Breathing off too much CO2: respiratory alkalosis, or the lungs offsetting a metabolic acidosis.

bands.label: High: acidotic
bands.note: Retaining CO2 from hypoventilation: respiratory acidosis, or the lungs offsetting a metabolic alkalosis.

bands.label: Low: acidotic
bands.note: Base lost or used up: metabolic acidosis, or the kidneys offsetting a respiratory alkalosis.

bands.label: High: alkalotic
bands.note: Base gained or acid lost: metabolic alkalosis, or the kidneys offsetting a respiratory acidosis.

figures.title: The four acid-base imbalances
figures.caption: Start from the cause: breathing problems change CO2 (respiratory), while acid or base gained or lost elsewhere changes bicarbonate (metabolic). The lungs compensate within minutes; the kidneys take days. Acidosis tends to raise potassium, alkalosis to lower it.
rows: Respiratory acidosis
Hypoventilation: COPD, opioid or sedative overdose, airway blockage, weak chest muscles
Slow shallow breathing, drowsiness, headache, confusion; potassium may rise
Respiratory alkalosis
Hyperventilation: anxiety or panic, pain, fever, early hypoxia, high ventilator rate
Rapid deep breathing, lightheadedness, tingling around the mouth and fingers, palpitations
Metabolic acidosis
DKA, severe diarrhea, kidney failure, lactic acid from shock or sepsis, aspirin overdose
Kussmaul breathing as the lungs blow off CO2, headache, confusion, warm flushed skin
Metabolic alkalosis
Vomiting, nasogastric suction, loop or thiazide diuretics, too much antacid or bicarbonate
Low potassium, muscle cramps, tingling, tetany; slow shallow breathing to retain CO2

figures.title: SIADH and diabetes insipidus
figures.caption: Mirror images of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). SIADH holds water, so urine is scant and concentrated while sodium falls; DI loses water, so urine is huge and dilute while sodium rises. Track daily weight and intake and output in both.
rows: ADH
Too much: the kidneys hold on to water
Too little, or the kidneys ignore it: water pours out
Urine
Scant and concentrated; specific gravity above 1.030
Large volumes, pale and dilute; specific gravity below 1.005
Serum sodium
Low (diluted), below 135 mEq/L
High, above 145 mEq/L, if intake cannot keep up
Osmolality
Low (blood diluted)
High (blood concentrated)
Client shows
Weight gain without edema; headache, confusion, seizures as sodium falls
Intense thirst, dehydration, weight loss, low BP
Common causes
Lung cancer (small cell), head injury, meningitis, some drugs such as SSRIs
Head injury or pituitary surgery (central); lithium (kidney type)
Treatment
Restrict fluids, daily weights, seizure precautions; hypertonic saline if severe
Replace fluids; desmopressin for central DI, then watch for water retention

figures.title: DKA and HHS
figures.caption: Both are high-glucose emergencies with severe dehydration; only DKA adds ketones and acidosis. IV fluids come first in both, and potassium is checked before insulin starts, because insulin drives potassium into the cells.
rows: Typical client
Type 1 diabetes, often younger; infection or missed insulin
Type 2 diabetes, often older; infection or poor fluid intake
Onset
Fast: hours to a day
Slow: days to weeks
Glucose
Above 250 mg/dL
Above 600 mg/dL, often far higher
Ketones
Present in blood and urine
Absent or minimal
pH
Below 7.30, with low bicarbonate: metabolic acidosis
Above 7.30: little or no acidosis
Hallmark signs
Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath, abdominal pain, vomiting
Extreme dehydration, confusion, seizures, coma; serum osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg
First priority
IV 0.9% saline, then IV regular insulin once potassium is 3.3 mEq/L or higher
IV 0.9% saline, often more than in DKA, then IV regular insulin
During treatment
Potassium falls fast; add dextrose to the IV as glucose nears 200 to 250 mg/dL
Lower glucose and sodium gradually; watch neuro status for cerebral edema

figures.title: Hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism
figures.caption: Everything slows in hypothyroidism and speeds up in hyperthyroidism. Too much levothyroxine produces hyperthyroid signs: rapid pulse, tremor, insomnia, heat intolerance. Give sedatives and opioids cautiously to a hypothyroid client.
rows: Metabolism
Slowed: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance
Racing: weight loss despite hunger, heat intolerance, sweating
Heart
Slow pulse, low body temperature
Rapid pulse, palpitations, atrial fibrillation
Skin, hair, eyes
Dry cool skin, coarse hair, puffy face
Warm moist skin, fine hair, bulging eyes (Graves)
Mind and bowels
Slow thinking, depression, constipation
Anxiety, tremor, insomnia, frequent stools
Labs (thyroid cause)
TSH high, free T4 low
TSH low, free T4 high
Treatment
Levothyroxine for life, on an empty stomach, same time daily
Methimazole or PTU, a beta-blocker for symptoms, radioactive iodine or surgery
Emergency
Myxedema coma: hypothermia, slow breathing, stupor; airway, gentle warming, IV hormone
Thyroid storm: fever, severe tachycardia, agitation; cool, beta-blocker, antithyroid drug

figures.title: Addison disease and Cushing syndrome
figures.caption: Opposite pictures of cortisol. Long-term steroids cause Cushing features and shut down the adrenals, so they are tapered, never stopped abruptly. Clients with Addison disease need extra (stress) doses for illness, injury or surgery.
rows: Problem
Too little cortisol and aldosterone
Too much cortisol, most often from long-term steroids
Appearance
Weight loss, darkened (bronzed) skin
Moon face, buffalo hump, thin skin, purple striae
Fluid and BP
Dehydration, low BP, salt craving
Fluid retention, high BP
Labs
Sodium low, potassium high, glucose low
Sodium high, potassium low, glucose high
Main risks
Adrenal crisis with any stress: shock, confusion
Infection, poor healing, bone loss, mood swings
Treatment
Lifelong hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone; wear medical ID
Taper steroids to the lowest dose; surgery for a tumor
Emergency or key care
Crisis: IV hydrocortisone and 0.9% saline with dextrose, fast
Check glucose and weight, protect from infection and falls

figures.title: Fluid volume deficit and excess
figures.caption: A deficit concentrates the blood and urine; an excess dilutes them and backs fluid into the lungs and tissues. Daily weight is the most sensitive measure of change: same time, same scale, similar clothing. One kilogram is about 1 liter.
rows: Common causes
Vomiting, diarrhea, bleeding, fever, burns, diuretics, poor intake
Heart or kidney failure, too much IV fluid or sodium, SIADH, cirrhosis
Weight
Rapid loss
Rapid gain; report more than 2 to 3 lb (1 kg) in a day or 5 lb in a week
Pulse and BP
Rapid weak pulse, low BP, dizziness on standing, flat neck veins
Bounding pulse, high BP, distended neck veins
Lungs and skin
Clear lungs, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor
Crackles, shortness of breath, pitting edema
Urine
Scant and dark; specific gravity above 1.030
Dilute if the kidneys work; low specific gravity
Labs
Hematocrit and BUN high (concentrated); sodium may rise
Hematocrit and BUN low (diluted)
Nursing care
Oral or isotonic IV fluids, strict intake and output, fall precautions
Restrict fluid and sodium, diuretics, raise the head of the bed, strict intake and output

figures.title: Hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis
figures.caption: Both remove waste, fluid and potassium. Hemodialysis works fast, so its risks are low BP and disequilibrium; peritoneal dialysis is gentler and daily, and its big risk is peritonitis, first seen as cloudy effluent.
rows: How it works
Blood runs through an outside filter, about 3 to 4 hours, 3 times a week
Dialysate fills the abdomen, dwells, then drains; exchanges daily, often at home
Access
Arteriovenous fistula or graft in the arm, or a central dialysis catheter
Catheter tunneled into the abdomen
Protect it
Feel a thrill, hear a bruit; no BP, IV or blood draws in that arm
Mask and sterile technique for every connection; keep the exit site clean and dry
Before and after
Weigh before and after; hold antihypertensives and dialyzable drugs as ordered
Warm dialysate with dry heat, never a microwave; outflow should at least equal inflow
Complications
Low BP, cramps, bleeding; disequilibrium (headache, nausea, confusion)
Peritonitis, poor outflow (kinks, full bowel), hernia, high glucose from the dialysate
Report at once
No thrill or bruit: the access may be clotted
Cloudy effluent, abdominal pain, fever: send the effluent for culture

figures.title: Kidney function labs
figures.caption: Creatinine is the most reliable kidney marker. BUN also rises with dehydration and GI bleeding, so a BUN rising much faster than creatinine (ratio above 20 to 1) points away from the kidney. Check both before contrast or nephrotoxic drugs.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Usually low muscle mass; rarely a concern.

bands.label: High
bands.note: Filtration is falling. A rise of 0.3 or more within 48 hours signals acute kidney injury.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Overhydration, liver failure or a low-protein diet.

bands.label: High
bands.note: Kidney failure, or dehydration, GI bleeding or a high-protein load if creatinine is normal.

bands.label: Severe
bands.note: Below 15 is kidney failure. Metformin is contraindicated; avoid contrast and nephrotoxic drugs.

bands.label: Reduced
bands.note: Adjust drug doses. Hold metformin at the time of iodinated contrast and for 48 hours after.

bands.label: Mildly low
bands.note: Common with aging; a concern only with signs of kidney damage.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Oliguria: below 0.5 mL/kg/hr, about 30 mL/hr, for 2 hours or more. Report it.

figures.title: Fasting glucose and A1c
figures.caption: A1c reflects average glucose over the past 2 to 3 months, so it needs no fasting and a week of careful eating will not change it. Fasting glucose needs at least 8 hours without food. A 2-hour glucose tolerance reading of 200 or more also diagnoses diabetes.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Hypoglycemia: give 15 g of fast carbohydrate if the client can swallow.

bands.label: Prediabetes
bands.note: Weight loss and activity can delay or prevent diabetes.

bands.label: Diabetes
bands.note: 126 or more on two tests. Many adults with diabetes aim for 80 to 130 before meals.

bands.label: Prediabetes
bands.note: Lifestyle change now; recheck at least yearly.

bands.label: Diabetes range
bands.note: 6.5% or more diagnoses diabetes. Below 7% is the usual goal for adults with diabetes.

bands.label: Above goal
bands.note: Glucose has run high for months. Explore barriers and expect treatment to intensify.

figures.title: Diabetic foot care
figures.caption: Neuropathy takes away the warning pain gives, and poor circulation slows healing, so an unnoticed blister can become an ulcer, infection or amputation. Daily inspection is the most important habit.
rows: Inspect
Check both feet daily, soles and between the toes, with a mirror or a helper
Count on pain to reveal an injury
Wash
Lukewarm water, temperature checked first; dry well between the toes
Soak the feet or use hot water
Skin
Moisturize the tops and soles
Put lotion between the toes
Nails and calluses
Trim nails straight across; a podiatrist handles thick nails and calluses
Cut calluses or corns, or use razor blades or chemical removers
Shoes and socks
Closed, well-fitting shoes and clean cotton socks; check shoes inside first
Go barefoot, even at home, or break in new shoes for long stretches
Cold feet
Wear warm socks
Use heating pads, hot water bottles or electric blankets
Report
Any cut, blister, redness, swelling, drainage or odor
Wait for a sore to heal on its own
